opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've thought about quite a bit. I think a lot of industry right now is very focused on scaling: taking an existing recipe, like a large transformer trained on internet-scale data, and pushing it as far as it can go with more compute and more data. That's produced incredible results, and I don't want to downplay it. But the incentives there naturally pull toward incremental improvements on whatever the current dominant paradigm is, because that's what reliably ships products and moves benchmarks.

What I'm most excited about are questions that feel a bit more long-term and a bit riskier. For example, how do we build systems that can compose knowledge in new ways, that can reason and plan by iteratively refining their answers rather than just predicting the next token, and that can generalize to situations far outside their training distribution? A lot of my work on energy-based models and compositional generative modeling comes from that angle. These are ideas that might not beat the state of the art on a leaderboard tomorrow, but I think they could matter a lot in five or ten years.

In academia, you have the freedom to explore those directions without needing an immediate payoff. You can work with students who bring fresh perspectives, follow a strange result down a rabbit hole, and publish openly so the whole community can build on it. Compute is definitely a constraint, but I actually think it's a useful one. It forces you to think about efficiency and better algorithms rather than just throwing more resources at the problem.

So for me, academia is the place where I can ask the more fundamental questions about what intelligence needs beyond scale. Industry and academia are complementary, and I collaborate with people in industry a lot, but for the kind of research I want to do right now, academia feels like the right home.

r001.rationale: The candidate says industry incentives favor incremental work on the dominant paradigm because it ships products and moves benchmarks, but does not attribute narrowed research freedom specifically to the commercial success of current AI models.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss vision-language models or assess how close they are to visual intelligence.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes industry focus on scaling existing transformer recipes, but does not state that industry researchers are pressured to pursue LLM research despite doubting one LLM can solve everything.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the kinds of questions I care about right now don't fit neatly into what industry labs are optimizing for.

A lot of my work is about rethinking the foundations of how we build these systems: how you compose different models together, how you get agents to plan and reason over long horizons with world models, how generative models can be built in ways that aren't just scaling up one monolithic architecture. Those are questions where the payoff is uncertain and probably years out. In a big industry lab there's enormous pressure, understandably, to work on things that improve the next release. The scaling recipe works, so the rational move is to keep pushing it. But that also means there's less room to say, "I think the whole framing might be wrong, let me spend two years exploring an alternative."

Academia gives me that freedom. I can pick a problem because it's intellectually interesting, not because it's on a roadmap. I can work with students who bring their own ideas, and that collaboration is genuinely one of the best parts of the job. And there's a real openness to it: we publish everything, share code, and build on each other's work in a way that's gotten harder in industry as things have become more competitive and closed.

The other piece is that academia is one of the few places where it makes sense to work on things that are actually hard to monetize. If an idea doesn't pan out, that's fine, that's part of the process. And if it does pan out, it tends to benefit everybody, not just one company.

I'll say the obvious caveat: compute is a real constraint. We can't train the biggest models. But I actually think that's a healthy pressure. It forces you to be clever, to ask whether there's a smarter way to get a capability rather than just throwing more resources at it. Historically, a lot of the ideas that eventually scaled came from people who didn't have the resources to scale and had to think differently. So I see that constraint as part of the point rather than purely a downside.

r002.rationale: The response makes no claim about vision-language models or their distance from actual visual intelligence.

r003.rationale: The response discusses pressure to improve releases and alternatives to monolithic architectures, but does not say researchers are pushed toward LLM research despite doubting that one LLM can solve everything.

astra-6.text:
For me, the main appeal of academia is the freedom to pursue open-ended questions. You can work on an idea because you think it could be important in the long run, even if you don’t yet know what the application will be or whether it will work. Industry has tremendous resources, but there’s often more pressure to connect research to a particular product or direction.

I also really enjoy working with students. They bring different perspectives and challenge your assumptions, and that can lead you toward questions you wouldn’t have thought to ask. So, for the kind of exploratory research I want to do, academia feels like a good fit right now.

r001.rationale: The response mentions product or directional pressure in industry, but does not attribute reduced research freedom to the commercial success of current AI models.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the main attraction is the freedom to explore questions that might take a long time to pay off. I’m interested in how we build more general intelligence—systems that can understand the world, reason about it, and act in it. There are still a lot of fundamental questions there, and I want the flexibility to try different approaches, including ones that don’t immediately lead to a product.

Industry has tremendous advantages in compute and engineering, but academia gives me more room to set my own research direction. I also really enjoy working with students. You get people coming in with different perspectives, and that can lead you toward ideas you wouldn’t have considered on your own. For the kind of exploratory research I want to do right now, that’s a very appealing environment.
